question: How do you say I am hungry in Hindi?
answer: **मुझे भूख लगी है** (mujhe bhookh lagi hai). Literally that is "to me hunger has attached" — Hindi treats hunger as something that happens to you, not something you are. Saying *main bhookha hoon* is understood but sounds like a translation.
body:
## Why the grammar looks backwards

A whole family of everyday feelings works this way in Hindi: hunger, thirst, cold, fever, even liking something. The person is the *recipient*, not the subject.

- मुझे भूख लगी है — I am hungry
- मुझे प्यास लगी है — I am thirsty
- मुझे ठंड लग रही है — I am cold

Once you notice the shape, all of them arrive at once.

## In a restaurant

You will more often need **खाना चाहिए** (khaana chahiye) — food is needed. Short, polite, and it works anywhere.

question: How do you say goodbye in Hindi?
answer: नमस्ते (namaste) is goodbye as well as hello — the same word does both, and it is never wrong. फिर मिलेंगे (phir milenge) means "we will meet again" and is the warm, ordinary way to leave. अलविदा (alvida) is a real word but a heavy one: it carries finality, so Hindi speakers save it for partings that matter and most learners should avoid it entirely.
body:
## The one that always works

नमस्ते. It opens a conversation and it closes one. Palms together, slight dip of the head, done. Nobody has ever been thought rude for saying namaste on the way out.

## What people actually say

- **फिर मिलेंगे** (phir milenge) — "we'll meet again". Neutral, friendly, correct with almost anyone.
- **चलता हूँ** (chalta hoon) if you are male, **चलती हूँ** (chalti hoon) if female — literally "I'm off". Casual, very common, slightly abrupt with an elder.
- **बाय** (bye) — yes, really. Urban India uses English "bye" constantly, and no one will think less of you.

## The word to be careful with

अलविदा (alvida) is what films use when someone is leaving for good. Using it to end a Tuesday lesson is like saying "farewell" to a colleague at 5pm — grammatically fine, tonally strange.

## Adding respect

Attach जी (ji): नमस्ते जी. One syllable, noticeably warmer. It works on almost any greeting in Hindi and is the cheapest politeness upgrade in the language.

question: How do you count to 100 in Hindi?
answer: Hindi numbers are learnt, not built. English gives you twenty-one from "twenty" plus "one"; Hindi gives you इक्कीस (ikkis), which you simply have to know. There are effectively 100 separate words. The good news is that the tens are regular, patterns rhyme in blocks, and most conversation only ever needs 1–20, the round tens, and prices.
body:
## Why this is harder than it looks

Most languages let you assemble numbers. Hindi largely does not. 21 is *ikkis*, 22 is *baais*, 23 is *teis* — each one an independent word, worn down over centuries from Sanskrit compounds.

## Start with these

**1–10:** एक ek, दो do, तीन teen, चार chaar, पाँच paanch, छह chhah, सात saat, आठ aath, नौ nau, दस das

**The tens:** दस das (10), बीस bees (20), तीस tees (30), चालीस chaalees (40), पचास pachaas (50), साठ saath (60), सत्तर sattar (70), अस्सी assee (80), नब्बे nabbe (90), सौ sau (100)

## The trick that saves you

Within each block of ten, the ending rhymes with the coming ten, not the current one. 29 is उनतीस (untees) — it leans on *tees* (30), not *bees* (20). Same for 39 (उनतालीस, untaalees), 49, and so on. Once you hear that, the nines stop feeling random.

## What you actually need first

Numbers 1–20, the round tens, and सौ (100) and हज़ार (thousand). That covers prices, ages, times and phone numbers — which is most of what a number is for in a conversation.

## In shops

Prices are usually said in full: दो सौ पचास (do sau pachaas) is 250. Listen for सौ (hundred) as the pivot; everything before it is the multiplier and everything after is the remainder.

question: What are the days of the week in Hindi?
answer: सोमवार somvaar (Monday), मंगलवार mangalvaar (Tuesday), बुधवार budhvaar (Wednesday), गुरुवार guruvaar (Thursday), शुक्रवार shukravaar (Friday), शनिवार shanivaar (Saturday), रविवार ravivaar (Sunday). Every one ends in -वार (-vaar), meaning "day", and each is named after a planet — exactly as the English days are, which is why the two sets line up perfectly.
body:
## The pattern that makes them easy

Strip -वार off and what remains is a planet. Som is the Moon, Mangal is Mars, Budh is Mercury, Guru is Jupiter, Shukra is Venus, Shani is Saturn, Ravi is the Sun.

Now compare English: Monday is Moon-day, Saturday is Saturn's day, Sunday is Sun's day. Both systems inherited the same Babylonian week. You are not memorising seven random words — you are matching two lists you half know already.

## Saying "on Monday"

Add को (ko): सोमवार को (somvaar ko) means "on Monday". Same particle for every day.

## Today, tomorrow, yesterday

- आज (aaj) — today
- कल (kal) — **both** tomorrow and yesterday
- परसों (parson) — **both** the day after tomorrow and the day before

This surprises everyone. The verb tense tells you which: *kal aaya* (kal + past) is yesterday, *kal aayega* (kal + future) is tomorrow. Hindi treats "one day away" as the unit and lets the sentence supply the direction.

## Booking a lesson

"मंगलवार को शाम सात बजे" (mangalvaar ko shaam saat baje) — Tuesday at 7 in the evening. Day + को + time + बजे is the whole formula.
keywords: days of week in hindi, hindi days, somvaar, hindi weekdays, monday in hindi

question: How do you tell the time in Hindi?
answer: Use बजे (baje) for the hour: तीन बजे (teen baje) is three o'clock. Half past is साढ़े (saadhe) before the hour — साढ़े तीन is 3:30 — but half past one and two are irregular, डेढ़ (dedh) and ढाई (dhai). Quarter past is सवा (sawa) and quarter to is पौने (paune), both placed before the hour.
body:
## The four words that cover most times

- **बजे** (baje) — o'clock. *paanch baje*, five o'clock.
- **सवा** (sawa) — quarter past. *sawa paanch*, 5:15.
- **साढ़े** (saadhe) — half past. *saadhe paanch*, 5:30.
- **पौने** (paune) — quarter to. *paune chhah*, 5:45 — note it counts toward SIX, not five.

That last one catches people out. पौने is "three quarters of", so it always names the hour you are approaching.

## The two you must simply memorise

- **डेढ़** (dedh) — 1:30. Not *saadhe ek*.
- **ढाई** (dhai) — 2:30. Not *saadhe do*.

These two are ancient contractions and there is no logic to recover. Everything from 3:30 onward is regular.

## Minutes

बजकर (bajkar) for past, बजने में (bajne mein) for to:
*paanch bajkar bees minute* — twenty past five.

In practice most people round to the nearest quarter and use the words above.

## Morning, afternoon, evening, night

सुबह (subah), दोपहर (dopahar), शाम (shaam), रात (raat) — placed **before** the time: शाम सात बजे, seven in the evening. Hindi rarely uses a 24-hour clock in speech, so this is how you avoid ambiguity.

## Booking a lesson

"क्या हम साढ़े छह बजे कर सकते हैं?" — can we do 6:30? Worth learning as a block; it is the sentence you will use most with a tutor.
keywords: time in hindi, how to tell time in hindi, baje meaning, saadhe hindi, hindi clock

question: What are the months and seasons in Hindi?
answer: Everyday Hindi uses the English month names, pronounced with Hindi sounds — जनवरी (janvari), फ़रवरी (farvari), मार्च (maarch). There is also a traditional Hindu calendar with its own months (चैत्र, वैशाख…), but those appear in festivals and almanacs rather than in conversation. The six seasons, however, are used constantly and have no English equivalent.
body:
## Months: use the English ones

In speech, on forms, in shops — जनवरी, फ़रवरी, मार्च, अप्रैल, मई, जून, जुलाई, अगस्त, सितंबर, अक्टूबर, नवंबर, दिसंबर. Learn to *read* them in Devanagari and you are done.

The traditional months (Chaitra, Vaishakh, Jyeshtha…) run on a lunisolar calendar and matter for festivals. Holi falls in Phalgun; Diwali in Kartik. You do not need them to speak, but you will meet them the first time someone explains a festival date.

## Seasons: six, not four

This is the part worth learning, because it is genuinely different.

- **वसंत** (vasant) — spring
- **ग्रीष्म** (greeshm) — summer
- **वर्षा** (varsha) — the monsoon
- **शरद** (sharad) — early autumn, after the rains
- **हेमंत** (hemant) — pre-winter
- **शिशिर** (shishir) — deep winter

Six seasons of two months each. It maps the north Indian year far better than four does, and the monsoon in particular is not a season English has a word for.

## In conversation

Most people say मौसम (mausam, weather) and name three: गर्मी (garmi, the hot season), सर्दी (sardi, the cold one), बरसात (barsaat, the rains). Learn those three first — they are what you will actually hear.

## Saying "in January"

जनवरी में (janvari mein). में covers "in" for months, years and seasons alike.

question: What are the colours in Hindi?
answer: लाल laal (red), नीला neela (blue), हरा hara (green), पीला peela (yellow), काला kaala (black), सफ़ेद safed (white), नारंगी naarangi (orange), गुलाबी gulaabi (pink), भूरा bhoora (brown), बैंगनी baingani (purple). Most colours ending in -आ change with gender: लाल stays लाल, but हरा becomes हरी for a feminine noun.
body:
## The gender rule, in one line

Colours ending in **-आ** change: हरा (hara) → हरी (hari) → हरे (hare). Colours ending in anything else — लाल, सफ़ेद, नारंगी, गुलाबी — never change at all.

So: हरा आम (green mango, masculine) but हरी मिर्च (green chilli, feminine). Same colour, different ending, because the *noun* decided.

## Colours named after things

Hindi is lovely about this and it makes them easy to remember:

- **नारंगी** (naarangi) — orange, from नारंगी the fruit
- **गुलाबी** (gulaabi) — pink, from गुलाब, a rose
- **बैंगनी** (baingani) — purple, from बैंगन, an aubergine
- **सुनहरा** (sunahra) — golden, from सोना, gold

Once you know the noun, the colour is free.

## Light and dark

हल्का (halka) for light, गहरा (gehra) for dark, placed before: हल्का नीला, light blue. Both follow the same -आ gender rule.

## Asking

"यह किस रंग का है?" (yeh kis rang ka hai?) — what colour is this? रंग (rang) is the word for colour, and it is the same रंग in Holi, the festival of colours.

question: What are the family words in Hindi?
answer: Hindi has a separate word for nearly every relative, because the relationship itself is built into the word. चाचा is your father's younger brother, ताऊ his elder brother, मामा your mother's brother, फूफा your father's sister's husband. English flattens all four into "uncle". This is not decoration — using the wrong one tells people something factually incorrect about your family.
body:
## The core

- **माँ / माता जी** (maa / mata ji) — mother
- **पिता जी / पापा** (pita ji / papa) — father
- **भाई** (bhai) — brother
- **बहन** (behen) — sister
- **बेटा / बेटी** (beta / beti) — son / daughter
- **पति / पत्नी** (pati / patni) — husband / wife

## Where it gets specific

**Your father's side:**
- चाचा (chacha) — father's younger brother; his wife is चाची
- ताऊ (taau) — father's elder brother; his wife is ताई
- बुआ (bua) — father's sister; her husband is फूफा

**Your mother's side:**
- मामा (mama) — mother's brother; his wife is मामी
- मौसी (mausi) — mother's sister; her husband is मौसा

**Grandparents:**
- दादा / दादी — father's parents
- नाना / नानी — mother's parents

## Why it is worth the effort

Say "mere mama" and every Hindi speaker instantly knows the person is on your mother's side. That is information English simply cannot carry in one word. In a culture where family structure matters, the vocabulary reflects it.

## The shortcut nobody minds

Older strangers get भैया (bhaiya, brother), दीदी (didi, sister), अंकल or आंटी. Age-appropriate, universally accepted, and it buys you time while you learn the real ones.
keywords: family words in hindi, hindi family members, chacha mama difference, hindi relatives, rishte hindi

question: What are the body parts in Hindi?
answer: सिर sir (head), आँख aankh (eye), नाक naak (nose), कान kaan (ear), मुँह munh (mouth), हाथ haath (hand or arm), पैर pair (foot or leg), पेट pet (stomach), दिल dil (heart), बाल baal (hair). Two catch learners out: हाथ covers hand and arm together, and पैर covers foot and leg — Hindi does not always split the limb the way English does.
body:
## The list

**Head and face:** सिर (head), बाल (hair), आँख (eye), कान (ear), नाक (nose), मुँह (mouth), दाँत (tooth), जीभ (tongue), गला (throat)

**Body:** गर्दन (neck), कंधा (shoulder), हाथ (hand/arm), उँगली (finger), पेट (stomach), पीठ (back), पैर (foot/leg), घुटना (knee)

**Inside:** दिल (heart), दिमाग़ (brain), खून (blood)

## Plurals that trip people up

आँख becomes आँखें (aankhein) for eyes; कान stays कान. The -एं plural applies to feminine nouns, and body parts are split between genders with no shortcut. Learn each with its plural when you meet it.

## Saying it hurts

The construction is not "I have a headache" but "to me, head-pain is happening":

**मेरे सिर में दर्द है** (mere sir mein dard hai) — my head hurts.

Swap सिर for any body part and the sentence still works. दर्द (dard) is pain, and it is the same दर्द you have heard in a hundred Hindi songs.

## दिल is bigger than "heart"

Anatomically it is the heart. In use it is feeling, courage, appetite, will. दिल नहीं लग रहा — "my heart isn't settling" — means bored, restless, homesick. You will hear it constantly.
keywords: body parts in hindi, hindi body vocabulary, sir aankh naak, hindi anatomy words, dard hindi

question: How do you ask for directions in Hindi?
answer: The one sentence to memorise is …कहाँ है? (…kahaan hai?) — where is…? Point at a map or say the place name in front of it: स्टेशन कहाँ है? The answers you will hear back are सीधे (seedhe, straight), दाएँ (daayen, right), बाएँ (baayen, left) and पास (paas, near). Learn those four and you can follow most replies even when the rest goes past you.
body:
## Ask

- **…कहाँ है?** (kahaan hai) — where is…?
- **यहाँ से कितनी दूर है?** (yahaan se kitni door hai) — how far from here?
- **कैसे जाऊँ?** (kaise jaaoon) — how do I get there?
- **क्या यह रास्ता सही है?** (kya yeh raasta sahi hai) — is this the right way?

## Understand the answer

- **सीधे** (seedhe) — straight on
- **दाएँ** (daayen) — right
- **बाएँ** (baayen) — left
- **मुड़िए** (mudiye) — turn
- **पास** (paas) — near · **दूर** (door) — far
- **यहाँ** (yahaan) — here · **वहाँ** (vahaan) — there
- **सामने** (saamne) — opposite, in front
- **पीछे** (peechhe) — behind

"सीधे जाइए, फिर दाएँ मुड़िए" — go straight, then turn right. That is a complete, natural direction and you now understand it.

## A word of realism

Ask two people. In much of India it is considered unhelpful to say "I don't know", so you may get a confident answer from someone who is guessing. This is not dishonesty — it is a different idea of what politeness requires. Two matching answers is your confirmation.

## Useful places

स्टेशन (station), बस अड्डा (bus stand), बाज़ार (market), अस्पताल (hospital), होटल (hotel), बैंक (bank), शौचालय / टॉयलेट (toilet).

## The polite opener

Start with सुनिए (suniye) — "listen", but the courteous kind, like "excuse me". Then your question. It changes the whole tone of the exchange.

question: How do you order food in Hindi?
answer: …दीजिए (…deejiye) is the polite "please give me": एक चाय दीजिए, one tea please. For the bill, बिल दीजिए. To ask the price, कितने का है? (kitne ka hai?). And the sentence worth learning before any other if you have a dietary restriction: मुझे … नहीं चाहिए (mujhe … nahin chahiye) — I don't want …
body:
## Ordering

- **एक चाय दीजिए** — one tea, please
- **दो रोटी और दाल दीजिए** — two rotis and dal, please
- **मेन्यू दिखाइए** (menu dikhaiye) — show me the menu
- **बिल दीजिए** (bill deejiye) — the bill, please
- **पानी** (paani) — water. **बोतल बंद पानी** — bottled water.

दीजिए is the polite imperative and it works with any noun. It is the single highest-value word on this page.

## Saying how spicy

- **तीखा** (teekha) — spicy hot
- **कम तीखा** (kam teekha) — less spicy
- **तीखा नहीं** (teekha nahin) — not spicy

Say it when you order, not after. And know that "not spicy" is a relative measurement.

## Dietary needs — say these clearly

- **मैं शाकाहारी हूँ** (main shaakaahaari hoon) — I am vegetarian
- **मुझे प्याज़ लहसुन नहीं चाहिए** — no onion or garlic
- **मुझे … से एलर्जी है** (mujhe … se allergy hai) — I am allergic to …

शाकाहारी is widely understood and respected. If it is an allergy rather than a preference, use the allergy sentence — it is taken more seriously.

## Prices

**कितने का है?** — how much is it? Answers come in numbers, so the numbers page is the natural next one.

## Afterwards

बहुत स्वादिष्ट था (bahut swaadisht tha) — it was delicious. Say it to the person who cooked it and watch what happens.

question: What Hindi phrases do I need for travelling in India?
answer: About fifteen phrases cover most of a trip: a greeting, thank you, how much, where is, too expensive, I don't understand, and a handful of numbers. English works in airports, hotels and big-city restaurants; Hindi starts mattering at the station, in the market, in a shared taxi, and in every small town — which is where the trip actually happens.
body:
## The fifteen

**Basics**
- नमस्ते (namaste) — hello and goodbye
- शुक्रिया / धन्यवाद — thank you
- हाँ / नहीं (haan / nahin) — yes / no
- ठीक है (theek hai) — okay, fine, agreed

**Getting around**
- …कहाँ है? — where is …?
- कितनी दूर? (kitni door) — how far?
- रुकिए (rukiye) — stop, please
- चलिए (chaliye) — let's go

**Money**
- कितने का है? — how much?
- बहुत महँगा है (bahut mehnga hai) — that's very expensive
- कम कीजिए (kam keejiye) — make it less

**When stuck**
- मुझे समझ नहीं आया (mujhe samajh nahin aaya) — I didn't understand
- धीरे बोलिए (dheere boliye) — please speak slowly
- अंग्रेज़ी आती है? (angrezi aati hai) — do you speak English?
- मदद कीजिए (madad keejiye) — please help

## Why it is worth learning fifteen words

Prices change. Not always dramatically, but visibly. More than that, the temperature of the interaction changes — someone who greets you in Hindi is a guest rather than a tourist, and India responds to that distinction.

## The single best one

धीरे बोलिए. You will understand far more Hindi than you can produce, and the only thing standing between you and comprehension is speed. This sentence buys you the gap.

## What English covers

Airports, chain hotels, trains booked online, big-city restaurants, most under-30s in metros. What it does not cover: local buses, small-town markets, autorickshaws, rural anything — the parts people remember.
keywords: hindi phrases for travel, india travel hindi, basic hindi for tourists, useful hindi phrases, hindi for backpackers

question: How do you say "I am learning Hindi" in Hindi?
answer: मैं हिंदी सीख रहा हूँ (main hindi seekh raha hoon) if you are male, मैं हिंदी सीख रही हूँ (seekh rahi hoon) if you are female. The verb changes with the gender of the speaker, not the listener — which is the first real grammar shock for most English speakers, and the reason this one sentence teaches more than it looks.
body:
## The sentence, taken apart

- **मैं** (main) — I
- **हिंदी** — Hindi
- **सीख** (seekh) — learn, the verb stem
- **रहा / रही** (raha / rahi) — the continuous marker, and this is the part that carries gender
- **हूँ** (hoon) — am

## Why the gender is on the verb

In Hindi the verb agrees with the subject's gender. A man says *karta hoon*, a woman says *karti hoon*, for the identical action. It feels strange for about a week and then becomes automatic.

Get it wrong and you will still be understood perfectly. Nobody will correct you unkindly. But it is the single most audible marker of a beginner, so it is worth fixing early.

## Swap the verb, keep the frame

- मैं खाना बना रहा हूँ — I am cooking
- मैं किताब पढ़ रही हूँ — I am reading a book
- मैं काम कर रहा हूँ — I am working

Same skeleton every time: subject + object + verb stem + raha/rahi + hoon. Hindi puts the verb last, and once that clicks, long sentences stop being frightening.

## The one that gets you help

**मैं हिंदी सीख रहा हूँ, कृपया धीरे बोलिए** — I'm learning Hindi, please speak slowly.

Say that and almost anyone in India will slow down, simplify, and start helping you. It is the most useful sentence in this entire section.

## Related

- मुझे हिंदी नहीं आती (mujhe hindi nahin aati) — I don't know Hindi
- थोड़ी थोड़ी आती है (thodi thodi aati hai) — I know a little
- मैं समझ सकता हूँ, बोल नहीं सकता — I can understand, I can't speak. True for most learners for a long time, and worth being able to say.

question: What is the difference between Hindi and Sanskrit?
answer: Sanskrit is the ancient classical language of India; Hindi is a modern language descended from it, roughly as Italian descends from Latin. They share the Devanagari script and a great deal of vocabulary, which makes them look closer than they are. Sanskrit has eight noun cases and a famously complex grammar; Hindi has simplified almost all of it. Learning Sanskrit will not let you speak Hindi.
body:
## The relationship, plainly

Sanskrit → Prakrits → Apabhramsha → Hindi. Roughly two and a half thousand years of ordinary speech drifting away from a literary standard.

A useful comparison: Latin and Italian. An Italian speaker recognises a great deal of Latin and cannot read Cicero. That is about where a Hindi speaker stands with Sanskrit.

## Same script, different languages

Both are written in Devanagari, which is why they look so similar on the page. But English and French share an alphabet too.

## Grammar is where they part

| | Sanskrit | Hindi |
|---|---|---|
| Noun cases | eight | effectively two, plus postpositions |
| Verb forms | enormous | manageable |
| Word order | very free | subject-object-verb |
| Dual number | yes | no |

Sanskrit encodes relationships in word endings. Hindi uses small separate words — का, को, से, में — placed after the noun. That single shift is most of what makes Hindi learnable.

## Shared vocabulary

Words borrowed straight from Sanskrit are called **तत्सम** (tatsam) — धन्यवाद, विद्यालय, राष्ट्र. Words worn down over time are **तद्भव** (tadbhav) — दूध from दुग्ध, हाथ from हस्त.

Formal Hindi leans tatsam; conversational Hindi leans tadbhav and Persian. A news broadcast and a market conversation can feel like different registers of the same language, because in vocabulary terms they nearly are.

## Which should you learn?

To talk to people, travel, watch films, work in north India: Hindi. To read scripture, study philology or chant: Sanskrit. They are different projects, and Hindi is by a wide margin the easier of the two.
keywords: hindi vs sanskrit, difference between hindi and sanskrit, is sanskrit hindi, devanagari sanskrit hindi

question: What does "ji" mean in Hindi?
answer: जी (ji) is a respect marker with no English equivalent. Added after a name or title it makes it polite — नमस्ते जी, पापा जी, गांधी जी. On its own it means a soft "yes". Before हाँ or नहीं it makes them formal: जी हाँ, जी नहीं. It is the smallest word in Hindi and one of the most important.
body:
## The four jobs it does

**1. After a name — respect.**
शर्मा जी, दादी जी, गांधी जी. Attach it to almost any name and the sentence becomes courteous. Overusing it is not a mistake; omitting it with an elder can be.

**2. On its own — a polite yes.**
Someone calls your name, you answer "जी?" — meaning "yes?" or "you called?". Warmer than हाँ and much more common than learners expect.

**3. Before yes and no — formality.**
जी हाँ (ji haan) and जी नहीं (ji nahin). This is the easiest politeness upgrade in the whole language: two extra letters and a flat answer becomes a respectful one.

**4. After a greeting — warmth.**
नमस्ते जी. Small, and immediately noticeable.

## Where it comes from

Probably from जीव, "life" or "soul" — so addressing the person, not the body. Whatever the etymology, it now functions as pure social lubricant.

## When not to use it

With close friends and children it sounds oddly stiff. Between peers of the same age it is unnecessary. The rule of thumb: elder, stranger, or anyone in a position of respect — use जी. Friend — do not.

## The learner's shortcut

If you are unsure how formal to be, add जी. Being slightly too polite in Hindi costs nothing. Being too casual with an elder is one of the few things that genuinely registers as rude.
keywords: ji meaning hindi, what does ji mean, hindi respect words, ji haan meaning, hindi politeness

question: When do you use ka, ki and ke in Hindi?
answer: का, की and के all mean "of" or possessive 's — and which one you use depends on the gender and number of the thing being POSSESSED, not the owner. राम का बेटा (Ram's son, masculine), राम की बेटी (Ram's daughter, feminine), राम के बेटे (Ram's sons, plural). The owner never changes the ending. Getting this backwards is the most common beginner mistake in Hindi.
body:
## The rule, stated once

Look at the noun **after** का/की/के. That noun decides.

- masculine singular → **का**
- feminine (singular or plural) → **की**
- masculine plural, or before a postposition → **के**

## Worked examples

- राम **का** बेटा — Ram's son (बेटा is masculine singular)
- राम **की** बेटी — Ram's daughter (बेटी is feminine)
- राम **के** बेटे — Ram's sons (plural masculine)
- सीता **का** बेटा — Sita's son. **Still का.** The owner is female and it changes nothing.

That last line is the whole lesson. Learners instinctively match the ending to the owner, because that is what English possessives feel like. Hindi does not care who owns it.

## With pronouns

मेरा / मेरी / मेरे (my), तुम्हारा / तुम्हारी / तुम्हारे (your), उसका / उसकी / उसके (his or her). Same three endings, same rule — and note उसका covers both "his" and "her", because again, the owner's gender is irrelevant.

मेरा नाम (my name — नाम is masculine), मेरी किताब (my book — किताब is feminine).

## Why it is worth drilling

का/की/के appear in almost every sentence of any length. Fix this and your Hindi immediately sounds several months more advanced. It is the highest-return grammar point in the language, and it is one rule.

## Quick self-test

तुम्हार__ बहन — your sister. बहन is feminine, so: तुम्हारी बहन.
keywords: ka ki ke hindi, hindi possessive, hindi grammar ka ki ke, mera meri mere, hindi postpositions

question: What is the word order in Hindi?
answer: Hindi is subject-object-verb: the verb goes last. "I eat rice" is मैं चावल खाता हूँ — literally "I rice eat". Adjectives come before nouns as in English, but the little joining words come AFTER the noun, which is why they are called postpositions rather than prepositions. Once the verb-last habit forms, long Hindi sentences stop feeling like puzzles.
body:
## SOV, and why it matters

English: I **eat** rice.
Hindi: मैं चावल **खाता हूँ** — I rice eat.

Around 45% of the world's languages do it this way, including Japanese, Korean and Turkish. English is the outlier, not Hindi.

The practical consequence: in a long Hindi sentence the verb — the thing that tells you what actually happened — arrives last. Listeners have to hold the whole sentence before it resolves. That is why Hindi feels fast to a beginner even at normal speed.

## Postpositions, not prepositions

English puts them before: **in** the house, **to** Ram, **from** Delhi.
Hindi puts them after: घर **में**, राम **को**, दिल्ली **से**.

The common ones: में (in), पर (on), से (from/with/by), को (to), का/की/के (of), तक (until), के लिए (for).

## Where the rest goes

- Adjective before noun: **लाल** किताब, red book — same as English
- Time and place early: **कल** मैं दिल्ली जाऊँगा — tomorrow I Delhi will-go
- Question words sit where the answer would: तुम **क्या** खा रहे हो? — you what eating are?

That last point is quietly useful. Hindi does not shuffle the sentence to ask a question the way English does.

## Flexibility

Word order can move for emphasis, because the postpositions keep the roles clear. चावल मैं खाता हूँ puts the stress on the rice. Beginners should stay with SOV until it is automatic; the freedom becomes available later.

## The habit to build

When you form a sentence, decide the verb last. Say the who, then the what, then the doing. Fight the English instinct for a fortnight and it stops being effortful.
keywords: hindi word order, hindi sentence structure, sov hindi, hindi grammar basics, postpositions hindi

question: What are the best Hindi movies for learning Hindi?
answer: Pick films with ordinary conversation rather than poetry or heavy dialogue: 3 Idiots, Queen, Piku, Dangal and Chhichhore all use everyday spoken Hindi at a followable pace. Watch with Hindi subtitles if you can read Devanagari, English subtitles if you cannot — and rewatch a favourite rather than starting a new film every time. Repetition is what actually moves listening forward.
body:
## Why film is genuinely useful

You get real speed, real register, real slang, and the emotional context that makes vocabulary stick. What a textbook cannot give you is the sound of someone irritated, teasing or in a hurry.

## Good starting films

- **3 Idiots** — clear dialogue, campus Hindi, widely subtitled
- **Queen** — a lot of simple everyday speech
- **Piku** — family conversation, wonderfully ordinary language
- **Dangal** — Haryanvi-flavoured, slower, very repetitive vocabulary
- **Chhichhore** — student slang, informal registers
- **Taare Zameen Par** — gentle pace, clear enunciation

## What to avoid at first

Period films and heavy poetic dialogue (much of Sanjay Leela Bhansali), anything leaning on Urdu-heavy shayari, and thrillers with mumbling. Beautiful, and not where to start.

## How to actually watch

1. First pass: English subtitles, just enjoy it.
2. Second pass: Hindi subtitles, pause on lines you almost caught.
3. Third pass: no subtitles for scenes you now know.

Rewatching one film three times beats watching three films once. The second viewing is where the learning happens.

## Series work too

**Panchayat** is the single best recommendation for learners — slow, rural, everyday Hindi, short episodes, and genuinely good. **Kota Factory** for student speech.

## The honest limit

Film Hindi will not teach you to speak. It builds listening, vocabulary and an ear for rhythm — and it will make you feel more fluent than you are, because recognition is easier than production. Pair it with someone who makes you talk.
keywords: hindi movies to learn hindi, best bollywood films for learners, learn hindi with movies, panchayat hindi

question: How can I practise speaking Hindi alone?
answer: You can build a great deal alone: shadowing, recording yourself, narrating your day out loud, and talking to a phone's voice keyboard. What you cannot do alone is find out what you are getting wrong — nothing free can hear you and correct you. The realistic plan is daily solo practice with one weekly session where a person interrupts you.
body:
## Things that genuinely work alone

**Shadowing.** Play a clip, then say the sentence along with it, matching speed and intonation. Two minutes a day rebuilds your mouth's habits faster than an hour of reading. This is the highest-value item on the page.

**Narrate your day.** Out loud, in Hindi, badly. मैं चाय बना रहा हूँ. मैं बाहर जा रहा हूँ. It sounds ridiculous and it converts passive vocabulary into words you can actually produce.

**Record yourself.** Sixty seconds on any topic, then listen back. It is uncomfortable and it is the fastest way to hear your own filler words and wrong verb endings.

**Dictation to your phone.** Set the keyboard to Hindi and speak. If the phone types what you meant, your pronunciation was clear enough. Free, instant, honest feedback on sounds — though not on grammar.

**Read aloud.** Any Devanagari text. It fixes the script and your mouth at once.

## What alone cannot do

You cannot correct an error you cannot hear. Learners plateau on the same handful of mistakes — a wrong gender ending, a flat retroflex ट, को where से belongs — and repeat them for months, becoming fluent at being wrong.

Voice apps do not catch this. A person catches it in ten seconds.

## The arrangement that works

Twenty minutes a day alone, one conversation a week with someone who interrupts you. Solo practice builds the material; the session finds the faults. Reverse the ratio and you waste the lesson on things you could have drilled yourself.

## If you have nobody yet

Language exchange partners are free and genuinely helpful for confidence. They are usually not teachers, so they will not know *why* something is wrong — but they will tell you when it is, and at the beginning that is most of the value.
keywords: practise hindi speaking alone, hindi speaking practice, shadowing hindi, learn hindi speaking at home

question: How is Hindi different from Punjabi and Bengali?
answer: All three are Indo-Aryan languages descended from Sanskrit, but they are separate languages, not dialects. Hindi uses Devanagari, Punjabi in India uses Gurmukhi, Bengali uses its own script. Grammar is broadly similar — verb last, postpositions, gendered nouns — but vocabulary and sound diverge enough that speakers cannot simply understand one another.
body:
## Mutual intelligibility, honestly

- **Hindi ↔ Punjabi**: partial. Shared vocabulary and a Hindi speaker in Delhi hears Punjabi constantly, so exposure does a lot of the work. A Hindi speaker with no exposure catches the gist and misses the detail.
- **Hindi ↔ Bengali**: low. Related, clearly, but a Hindi speaker does not follow a Bengali conversation.
- **Hindi ↔ Urdu**: essentially the same spoken language in different scripts. Genuinely different from the two above.

## Scripts

| Language | Script |
|---|---|
| Hindi | Devanagari देवनागरी |
| Punjabi (India) | Gurmukhi ਗੁਰਮੁਖੀ |
| Punjabi (Pakistan) | Shahmukhi, Perso-Arabic |
| Bengali | Bengali–Assamese বাংলা |

Devanagari and Bengali script share an ancestor and both hang letters from a horizontal line, which is why they look related at a glance.

## Grammar differences worth knowing

**Punjabi** is tonal — pitch changes meaning, which is unusual in this family and hard for Hindi speakers.

**Bengali** has **no grammatical gender at all.** No masculine and feminine nouns, no changing verb endings. For an English speaker that removes the single hardest part of Hindi. Bengali instead has an elaborate system of verb forms for politeness levels.

## Which is most useful?

By speakers and reach, Hindi — around 600 million, and it functions as a link language across north India. Bengali is next at roughly 265 million and gives you Bangladesh as well as West Bengal. Punjabi is the most useful of the three in the UK and Canada, where the diaspora is large.

## Does one help with another?

Some. Shared Sanskrit vocabulary and a shared grammatical shape mean the second Indo-Aryan language is noticeably easier than the first. But it is a real second language, not a dialect you can guess your way into.
keywords: hindi vs punjabi, hindi vs bengali, indian languages difference, indo aryan languages, which indian language to learn

question: How do you type in Hindi on a phone or computer?
answer: On a phone, add the Hindi keyboard in your settings and use the transliteration mode: type "namaste" and it offers नमस्ते. On Windows, add Hindi under Language settings and use the Hindi Phonetic layout. On Mac it is Input Sources → Devanagari – QWERTY. Transliteration is what almost everyone uses — you never have to learn a new key layout.
body:
## Android

Settings → System → Languages & input → Virtual keyboard → Gboard → Languages → add **Hindi (Latin)** for transliteration, or **Hindi** for the native layout.

Hindi (Latin) is the one you want. You type *kaise ho* and it offers कैसे हो.

## iPhone

Settings → General → Keyboard → Keyboards → Add New Keyboard → **Hindi (Transliteration)**.

Switch with the globe key.

## Windows

Settings → Time & Language → Language → Add a language → हिन्दी. Install it, then pick **Hindi Phonetic** as the keyboard. Switch with Windows + Space.

## Mac

System Settings → Keyboard → Input Sources → + → Hindi → **Devanagari – QWERTY**.

## Voice is often faster

Every one of these has a microphone. Speaking Hindi into it is quicker than typing and doubles as pronunciation practice — if the phone types what you meant, you said it clearly enough.

## The two characters worth knowing

- **Halant** ( ् ) removes the built-in "a" from a consonant. क is "ka"; क् is a bare "k". Transliteration handles this automatically, which is most of why it is easier.
- **Nukta** ( ़ ) marks borrowed sounds: ज → ज़ (za), फ → फ़ (fa).

## Just need your name?

Our [name in Hindi tool](../../name-in-hindi/) converts a name to Devanagari with no keyboard setup at all.
keywords: type hindi on phone, hindi keyboard, hindi typing, devanagari keyboard, transliteration hindi

question: What is the difference between Hindi and Urdu?
answer: In everyday speech there is almost none — a Hindi speaker and an Urdu speaker discussing food, family or the weather understand each other completely. The differences are the script (Devanagari versus a Perso-Arabic script written right to left) and the formal vocabulary, which Hindi draws from Sanskrit and Urdu from Persian and Arabic. Linguists often treat them as one language, Hindustani, with two literary standards.
body:
This is one of the most misunderstood questions about either language, and the answer matters practically: if you learn one, you have largely learned the other.

## The everyday language is the same

Take a normal sentence — asking for tea, telling someone you are tired, arranging to meet tomorrow. In Hindi and Urdu that sentence is word-for-word identical. Same grammar, same word order, same postpositions, same verb endings, same core vocabulary.

Bollywood films are the clearest evidence. They are watched without subtitles in both India and Pakistan because the dialogue is neither pure Hindi nor pure Urdu — it is the shared everyday register both audiences speak.

## The script is the real difference

**Hindi** uses Devanagari, written left to right, with every vowel marked.

**Urdu** uses a modified Perso-Arabic script written right to left, usually in the flowing Nastaliq style, and short vowels are generally not written at all — you supply them from knowing the word.

This is the difference that actually costs time. Someone fluent in spoken Urdu still needs several weeks to read Hindi, and vice versa.

## Formal vocabulary diverges

The higher the register, the further apart they get.

For "country", conversational speech uses **mulk** in both. Formal Hindi prefers **rashtra** from Sanskrit; formal Urdu prefers **mulk** from Arabic. In a news broadcast, a legal document or a poem, the two can become genuinely hard for the other's speaker to follow.

## The practical consequences for a learner

**If you speak Urdu, you already speak Hindi.** You need the script and some Sanskrit-derived formal vocabulary. That is weeks of work, not years.

**If you are learning from scratch, choose by purpose.** India and Bollywood point to Hindi. Pakistan, Islamic scholarship or Urdu poetry point to Urdu. For travel across South Asia generally, either works.

**Do not learn both scripts at once.** Pick one, get comfortable, then add the other. Learning two writing systems for one spoken language simultaneously is a well-known way to confuse yourself.

## A note on the politics

The split is more political than linguistic and became sharper after 1947. Before that, Hindustani in both scripts was widely understood as one language. Some people feel strongly about this. As a learner you do not have to take a position — but it is worth knowing the question is sensitive.
keywords: hindi vs urdu, difference hindi urdu, are hindi and urdu the same, hindustani language

question: What are the Hindi pronouns and when do you use tu, tum and aap?
answer: Hindi has three words for 'you' and choosing wrong is the fastest way to offend someone. आप (aap) is respectful and the safe default for any adult. तुम (tum) is familiar, for friends and people younger than you. तू (tu) is intimate or insulting depending entirely on the relationship — as a learner, never use it.
body:
Hindi pronouns are simple except for one thing, and that one thing matters enormously.

## The full set

| Person | Hindi | Romanised |
|---|---|---|
| I | मैं | main |
| we | हम | ham |
| you (respectful) | आप | aap |
| you (familiar) | तुम | tum |
| you (intimate) | तू | tu |
| he / she / it / that | वह | vah |
| this / he / she (near) | यह | yah |
| they / those | वे | ve |

## The three yous — this is the part that matters

**आप** — respectful. Use it for anyone older, anyone you have just met, teachers, officials, your partner's family, shopkeepers, and every stranger. **As a learner, use आप with everyone until someone invites you to do otherwise.** Nobody has ever been offended by too much respect.

**तुम** — familiar. Friends, colleagues your own age, people clearly younger. Wait to be invited, or wait until they use it with you first.

**तू** — intimate. Used with very small children, a spouse, a very old friend, or God in prayer. Used with anyone else it is a deliberate insult, and a foreigner using it by accident is genuinely shocking. Learn to recognise it; do not use it.

Japanese, Korean and German speakers will find this familiar. English speakers have nothing to map it onto and must simply learn it.

## No gender in the third person

वह means he, she and it. Hindi does not distinguish them. Whether a person is male or female shows up in the **verb**, not the pronoun — which is the opposite of English and takes some getting used to.

## Near and far

यह is "this" or a person nearby. वह is "that" or a person further away. Both are used for people constantly, which sounds impolite translated literally into English but is completely normal.

## The verb changes with the pronoun

तुम and आप take different verb forms, and आप always takes the plural form even when addressing one person — exactly like French *vous*. Getting the pronoun right and the verb wrong is a very common intermediate error.

## The one rule to take away

**Use आप.** Everything else can be learned slowly. Choosing the wrong "you" is the only pronoun mistake that will actually cause offence.
keywords: hindi pronouns, aap tum tu difference, hindi you formal informal, main tum aap

question: How do you say please and thank you in Hindi?
answer: Thank you is धन्यवाद (dhanyavaad) or the more everyday शुक्रिया (shukriya). Please is कृपया (kripaya), but in real speech Hindi rarely uses a separate word for please — politeness is built into the verb ending instead. Saying कृपया in casual conversation sounds oddly formal, like saying 'kindly' in English.
body:
This is a place where translating word-for-word from English produces something no Hindi speaker would say.

## Thank you

**शुक्रिया** — *shukriya* — from Arabic via Persian. Everyday, warm, used constantly. This is the one to learn first.

**धन्यवाद** — *dhanyavaad* — from Sanskrit. More formal, used in writing, speeches and official settings.

**बहुत बहुत धन्यवाद** — thank you very much.

## Please — and why you probably should not say it

**कृपया** — *kripaya* — exists, and is correct, and appears on signs and in announcements. In conversation it sounds stiff.

What Hindi does instead is build the politeness into the **verb**:

- बैठो — *baitho* — sit (to a friend)
- बैठिए — *baithiye* — please sit (polite)
- बैठिएगा — *baithiyega* — please do sit (very polite)

The **-iye** ending IS "please". Add कृपया on top and you have said please twice.

This is the single most useful thing on this page: learn the **-iye** form of the ten verbs you use most, and you will sound polite without ever needing the word for please.

## The other everyday courtesies

- **स्वागत है** — *swagat hai* — you're welcome
- **कोई बात नहीं** — *koi baat nahin* — no problem, don't mention it. Used far more than स्वागत है
- **माफ़ कीजिए** — *maaf kijiye* — sorry, excuse me
- **जी** — *ji* — added to a name or to yes/no, and worth more than any of the above

## A cultural note that saves confusion

Within close family, thanking someone for an ordinary kindness can sound cold — as though you are treating them as an outsider doing you a service. A mother handing you food does not expect शुक्रिया.

This does not apply to shops, restaurants, taxis or strangers, where thanking is completely normal. As a learner, thanking too much is a small and forgivable error. Do not overthink it.
keywords: thank you in hindi, please in hindi, shukriya dhanyavaad, hindi politeness

question: How does the verb 'to be' work in Hindi?
answer: होना (hona) is the most important verb in Hindi and it is irregular. In the present tense it has five forms: हूँ (hoon) for I, है (hai) for he/she/it and तू, हो (ho) for तुम, and हैं (hain) for we, they and आप. It goes at the end of the sentence, and unlike English it is never dropped.
body:
Learn this verb properly in week one. Everything else in Hindi grammar leans on it.

## The present tense

| Pronoun | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| मैं | हूँ *hoon* | मैं ठीक हूँ — I am fine |
| तू | है *hai* | तू कहाँ है — where are you |
| तुम | हो *ho* | तुम कैसे हो — how are you |
| आप | हैं *hain* | आप कैसे हैं — how are you (polite) |
| वह | है *hai* | वह डॉक्टर है — he/she is a doctor |
| हम / वे | हैं *hain* | हम तैयार हैं — we are ready |

Five forms, and हैं covers three of the pronouns. This is less than French or Spanish.

## It goes at the end

मैं भारत से हूँ — literally "I India from am".

The verb is last. Always. This is the word-order rule that costs English speakers their first few months, and होना 	is where you first meet it.

## Never drop it

Russian and Arabic drop the present tense of "to be" — "I student" is a complete sentence. Hindi does not. मैं छात्र without हूँ is incomplete and sounds wrong.

## The past tense, where gender arrives

था / थे / थी / थीं — *tha / the / thi / thin*

Now the verb agrees with **gender**, not just number:

- मैं था — I was (man speaking)
- मैं थी — I was (woman speaking)
- वे थे — they were (masculine or mixed)
- वे थीं — they were (all feminine)

This surprises people. In Hindi the verb tells you the speaker's gender, which no European language does in the same way.

## It builds every other tense

होना 	is the helper verb for the continuous and habitual tenses:

- मैं जा रहा हूँ — I am going
- मैं जाता हूँ — I go / I usually go

Get होना wrong and every tense after it is wrong. Get it right and the rest of the verb system is largely regular.

## There is no verb "to have"

Possession uses के पास with होना: मेरे पास किताब है — literally "near me a book is". Strange for a week, then straightforward.
keywords: hona hindi verb, to be in hindi, hai hain hoon, hindi present tense

question: What is the best way to learn Hindi as a complete beginner?
answer: Learn Devanagari first — four to eight weeks at twenty minutes a day — then start speaking badly immediately rather than waiting until you feel ready. The two things that most reliably separate people who learn Hindi from people who quit are starting the script early and being corrected by someone who knows what to listen for.
body:
There is no shortcut, but there is an order that works better than the order most people choose.

## Weeks 1 to 8: the script, twenty minutes a day

Do not postpone this. Romanised Hindi has no agreed spelling — the same word appears as *nahin*, *nahi*, *nahee* and *nhi* — so learning through romanisation means learning every word twice.

Learn the consonants as the **five-row grid**, not as a list. The rows are organised by where in the mouth the sound is made, so the grid teaches pronunciation at the same time as the shapes. Five rows of five is much less to memorise than 46 separate characters.

## From week 1, in parallel: speak badly

The biggest single predictor of whether someone reaches conversation is how early they start producing language. Not consuming — producing.

Say wrong things out loud from the first week. Learners who wait until they feel ready take roughly twice as long, and many never start at all.

## What to learn first, in order

1. होना — the verb "to be". Everything leans on it.
2. आप, तुम, मैं — and when to use each.
3. Numbers 1 to 20, then 20 to 100.
4. The postpositions का, को, से, में.
5. Twenty verbs in the polite **-iye** form.

That is roughly three months of material and it covers most everyday situations.

## The three things self-study cannot do

**Correct your pronunciation.** You cannot hear the difference between त and ट at first. An app will not tell you, and an uncorrected error becomes permanent in about six weeks.

**Correct your gender agreement.** Hindi verbs change with the speaker's gender, and getting it wrong sounds jarring to a native speaker in a way you will never notice yourself.

**Make you speak.** An app lets you feel productive while never producing a sentence under pressure.

## A realistic weekly plan

- **One hour** with a tutor who corrects you
- **Two twenty-minute sessions** on script and vocabulary
- **Ten minutes daily** of speaking out loud, even to yourself
- **One film or show a week** with subtitles, then without

Three hours a week gets most people to simple conversation in six to nine months.

## What to avoid

**Learning both Hindi and Urdu scripts at once.** Pick one.

**Grammar-first study.** ने will defeat you in month two if you meet it before you can hold a conversation. Leave it.

**Waiting to feel ready.** Nobody feels ready. That is not a stage that arrives.

question: What are the common Hindi greetings besides namaste?
answer: नमस्ते (namaste) works everywhere and at any time of day, which is why it is the one everyone learns. But Hindi speakers also use नमस्कार (namaskar) for more formal situations, आदाब (aadaab) in Urdu-influenced settings, सत श्री अकाल (sat sri akal) among Punjabis, and simply हाय 	or hello in cities among younger people.
body:
नमस्ते is never wrong, but using only नमस्ते marks you immediately as a learner. Here is what people actually say.

## The universal one

**नमस्ते** — *namaste* — works for hello and goodbye, morning and night, one person or a group. Palms together, a slight bow of the head. If you learn one greeting, learn this.

**नमस्कार** — *namaskar* — the same word, more formal. Used in speeches, on the news, and with someone considerably older or more senior.

## By community and region

**आदाब** — *aadaab* — used in Urdu-speaking and Muslim contexts, with a hand raised towards the forehead. Widely understood in Delhi, Lucknow and Hyderabad.

**सत श्री अकाल** — *sat sri akal* — the Punjabi Sikh greeting. Used constantly in Punjab, Delhi and across the Punjabi diaspora.

**राम राम** — *ram ram* — rural north India, particularly among older people. Warm and traditional.

**जय श्री कृष्ण** — *jai shri krishna* — common in Gujarat and among Vaishnav communities.

## Time of day

These exist and are grammatically correct, but they are translations from English and sound slightly formal or media-flavoured in speech:

- सुप्रभात — good morning
- शुभ रात्रि — good night

Most people say नमस्ते instead, or in cities simply "good morning" in English.

## What people under thirty actually say in cities

**हाय**, **hello**, **hi** — English greetings are completely normal in urban India among friends and colleagues. Using नमस्ते with a 22-year-old colleague in Bangalore is not wrong, but it may feel formal to them.

## The follow-up, which matters more than the greeting

Nobody stops at hello. Learn these:

- **आप कैसे हैं?** — how are you (to a man, polite)
- **आप कैसी हैं?** — how are you (to a woman, polite)
- **क्या हाल है?** — what's up (casual)
- **ठीक हूँ, आप सुनाइए** — I'm fine, tell me about you

Note that the "how are you" form **changes with the gender of the person you are asking**. This is the kind of detail that self-study misses and a tutor catches in the first lesson.

## The safe default

नमस्ते with जी added to a name — नमस्ते शर्मा जी — is polite everywhere in India with everyone, and nobody has ever taken offence at it.

question: Can I learn Hindi without learning the Devanagari script?
answer: Yes, and for some goals it is the right choice — if you only want to speak with family or handle a trip, spoken Hindi through romanisation is a legitimate path and no tutor should refuse it. But it costs you more than people expect: romanised Hindi has no standard spelling, so you end up learning many words twice, and almost all good material beyond beginner level is in Devanagari.
body:
This question is usually asked apologetically, as though skipping the script is cheating. It is not. But the trade-off is real and worth seeing clearly before you choose.

## When skipping the script is genuinely reasonable

**You want to talk to your in-laws.** Spoken comprehension and production. You will never need to read a menu.

**You are going to India for three weeks.** Two hundred spoken phrases will serve you far better than four weeks on the alphabet.

**You already speak Urdu.** You have the language; you are choosing which script to add, and Nastaliq may be more useful to you.

**You have dyslexia or a visual impairment** that makes a new script genuinely costly.

In all of these, say so in your first lesson. A tutor who insists on the alphabet regardless is not listening to you.

## What it actually costs

**Romanisation has no standard.** नहीं is written *nahin*, *nahi*, *nahee*, *nheen* and *nhi*, all in common use. You learn a word, meet it spelled differently, and do not recognise it. This is the largest hidden cost and it compounds.

**Romanisation cannot show the sounds that matter.** त and ट are both written "t". द and ड are both "d". These are different letters that change meaning, and the romanisation erases the distinction — so you cannot even see that there is something to hear. This is the deepest problem.

**Material dries up fast.** Beginner phrasebooks are romanised. Almost nothing at intermediate level is. You will hit a wall around month six with nothing to read.

**You cannot use a dictionary properly.** Hindi dictionaries are ordered by Devanagari.

## The middle path most people should take

**Learn to READ Devanagari without learning to WRITE it.**

Reading is about four to eight weeks at twenty minutes a day. Handwriting is a separate skill that takes months and that you may genuinely never need — typing exists.

This gets you dictionaries, signage, subtitles, real materials and the ability to see the retroflex distinction, at a fraction of the cost.

## If you still choose to skip it

Be consistent. Pick one romanisation system and stick to it, ideally IAST or your tutor's, and write your own notes the same way every time. Most of the pain comes from inconsistency rather than from romanisation itself.

And revisit the decision at month three. Many people who skip the script find that once they can hold a simple conversation, the alphabet suddenly looks like four weeks well spent rather than a barrier at the start.
